rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Explain the following reactions :
(a) Clemmensen reduction
(b) Stephen reaction
rows.solution:
(a) CLEMMENSEN REDUCTION converts the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone all the way to a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group, using ZINC AMALGAM and CONCENTRATED HYDROCHLORIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}/\text{conc. }\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

For example, propanone gives propane and benzaldehyde gives toluene.

Note that neither hydride reagents nor catalytic hydrogenation will do this — they stop at the ALCOHOL. Removing the oxygen entirely needs either Clemmensen or the Wolff-Kishner reduction, and the choice between them turns on conditions: Clemmensen works in strong ACID, Wolff-Kishner in strong ALKALI, so a compound sensitive to one is reduced by the other.

(b) STEPHEN REACTION converts a NITRILE to an ALDEHYDE, using tin(II) chloride and hydrochloric acid. The nitrile is reduced only as far as the IMINE, which is then hydrolysed:
\(\mathrm{R{-}CN} + \mathrm{SnCl_2} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}CH{=}NH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{R{-}CHO} + \mathrm{NH_3}\)

Ethanenitrile, for instance, gives ethanal.

Again the point is STOPPING at the right stage: lithium aluminium hydride would carry the reduction on to the primary amine. Diisobutylaluminium hydride, DIBAL-H, achieves the same halt by a different route.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the IUPAC name of the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_6]Cl_4}\)
(ii) On the basis of crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion, if \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\).
(iii) What are Heteroleptic complexes?
rows.solution:
(i) The six ammine ligands are neutral and four chlorides sit outside, so the complex cation carries \(+4\) and platinum is \(+4\). The complex is the CATION, so it takes no \(-\mathrm{ate}\) suffix, and the counter ion is named last:
HEXAAMMINEPLATINUM(IV) CHLORIDE

Note the double "m" in ammine, which distinguishes the ligand ammonia from an organic amine.

(ii) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

With \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) — a WEAK FIELD — promotion is the cheaper option, so the FOURTH electron goes upstairs rather than pairing. All four remain unpaired: a HIGH SPIN complex with \(\mu = 4{\cdot}90\) B.M.

(iii) A HETEROLEPTIC complex is one in which the metal is bound to MORE THAN ONE KIND of ligand.

Examples: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^+}\), with both ammine and chlorido ligands, and \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\).

The contrast is a HOMOLEPTIC complex, bound to only one kind — \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\), for instance. The distinction matters for isomerism: only a HETEROLEPTIC complex can show geometrical isomerism, since there must be different ligands for their arrangement to differ.

rows.stem:
(i) Using IUPAC norms write the formulas for the following :
(i.i) Pentaamminenitrito-N-Cobalt (III)
(i.ii) Tetrahydroxidozincate (II)
(ii) What is crystal field splitting energy ?
rows.solution:
(i)(i.i) PENTAAMMINENITRITO-N-COBALT(III).

Work out the charge from the name. Cobalt is \(+3\), as the bracket states; the five ammine ligands are neutral; the nitrito ligand is the nitrite ion and gives \(-1\). The total is \(+2\):
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\)

The "N" records that the cobalt is bonded to the NITROGEN of the ambidentate nitrite. Bound through oxygen instead it would be the nitrito-O isomer, a linkage isomer of the same formula and a different colour.

(i.ii) TETRAHYDROXIDOZINCATE(II).

The \(-\mathrm{ate}\) suffix says the complex is an ANION. Zinc is \(+2\) and four hydroxide ligands give \(-4\), so the ion carries \(-2\):
\(\mathrm{[Zn(OH)_4]^{2-}}\)

This is the ion formed when zinc or its hydroxide dissolves in excess alkali — the reaction that makes zinc amphoteric.

(ii) CRYSTAL FIELD SPLITTING ENERGY is the ENERGY SEPARATION between the two sets of d orbitals produced when a ligand field surrounds the metal ion — between the \(t_{2g}\) and \(e_g\) levels in an octahedral complex. It is written \(\Delta_0\) for octahedral and \(\Delta_t\) for tetrahedral.

In a free ion the five d orbitals are of EQUAL energy. Ligands approaching from particular directions repel the electrons in orbitals pointing towards them more than those in orbitals pointing between, so the degeneracy is lifted.

The size of \(\Delta_0\) depends on the ligand — the spectrochemical series arranges them by it — and it decides two things: the COLOUR of the complex, since a d-d transition absorbs a photon of exactly that energy, and whether the complex is HIGH or LOW SPIN, according to whether \(\Delta_0\) is smaller or greater than the pairing energy.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following statements :
(a) Scandium (Z=21) is a transition element but Zn (Z=30) is not.
(b) \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)]^{3+}}\) is coloured while \(\mathrm{[Sc(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) is colourless.
(c) Physical and chemical properties of the 4d and 5d series of the transition elements are quite similar than expected.
rows.solution:
(a) Because of the d subshell in the ATOM, not the ion.

A transition element is defined as one with a PARTLY FILLED d subshell in the neutral atom OR in at least one of its stable ions — and either route is enough.

Scandium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1 4s^2\), so its ATOM has a partly filled \(3d\) subshell. Its only ion, \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\), is \(3d^0\), but the atom already satisfies the definition.

Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\) and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — COMPLETELY FILLED in both the atom AND the ion, so neither route is open and zinc is excluded.

(b) Because titanium(III) has a d ELECTRON and scandium(III) has none.

Colour arises from a D-D TRANSITION, an electron absorbing visible light and jumping from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper. The jump needs an electron below and a vacancy above.

\(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\) — one electron and plenty of vacancies — so its aqueous ion is violet. \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\), with the argon configuration and no d electron at all, so no such jump is possible and its solutions are colourless.

(c) Because of the LANTHANOID CONTRACTION.

An element of the 5d series should be substantially larger than the 4d element above it, one whole period lower. It is not — zirconium and hafnium, for instance, have almost identical radii of about 160 pm.

The cause is the fourteen LANTHANOIDS that intervene before the 5d series begins. Across them each added electron enters an inner \(4f\) orbital, which shields poorly, so the rising nuclear charge pulls the outer shells inwards and cancels the increase expected from the extra period.

Since chemical behaviour depends largely on size and charge, the two series behave far more alike than their positions would suggest — and the pairs are correspondingly hard to separate.

rows.stem: A primary amine 'A' \(\mathrm{C_2H_7N}\) reacts with alkyl halide (\(\mathrm{C_2H_5I}\)) to give secondary amine 'B'. 'B' reacts with \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\) to give a solid 'C' which is insoluble in alkali. Identify 'A', 'B', 'C' and write all the chemical reactions involved.
rows.solution:
Take the clues in order.

'A' is a PRIMARY amine with the formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_7N}\), and only one structure fits:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), ethanamine

Reaction with iodoethane ALKYLATES the nitrogen, giving the secondary amine:
\(\mathrm{B} = (\mathrm{CH_3CH_2})_2\mathrm{NH}\), N-ethylethanamine
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2} + \mathrm{C_2H_5I} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} + \mathrm{HI}\)

Benzenesulphonyl chloride then gives the sulphonamide:
\(\mathrm{C} = (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{N{-}SO_2{-}C_6H_5}\), N,N-diethylbenzenesulphonamide
\((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NSO_2C_6H_5} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The INSOLUBILITY in alkali is the clue that confirms 'B' is SECONDARY, and it is the whole point of HINSBERG'S TEST. A primary amine's sulphonamide keeps one hydrogen on its nitrogen, made acidic by the two sulphonyl oxygens, so it DISSOLVES in alkali. A secondary amine's has no such hydrogen and stays a solid.
